asr.full_text: Hi, welcome back to our channel! As a result of the unprecedented Corona Virus pandemic, the government passed the $2 trillion coronavirus relief bill that promises to help Americans with this huge financial impact. The bill, known as the CARES Act, delivers payments to most taxpayers, vastly expands unemployment benefits, and makes testing for the virus free, among other provisions. So who can get this stimulus check? How much can you get? And when will you get it? Today, we're going to go over all the questions related to the stimulus check. Are you ready? Let's go! Before we start, I want to mention that the official term that the IRS uses is Economic Impact Payments. We're just gonna call it the stimulus check in this video. What the IRS uses is economic impact payments. We're just going to call it the stimulus check in this video. 1. Who will be eligible for the checks? In addition to American citizens, green card holders and workers with visas such as H1B, H2A, and E2 are eligible to receive the check. This includes individuals who are employed, unemployed, and self-employed. However, you have to meet two basic requirements. First, you have to have a social security number. And second, you must have filed your 2018 or 2019 tax returns. For households with mixed immigration status, where your spouse or a dependent child uses an individual taxpayer identification number. Unfortunately, no one in the household will qualify for the stimulus checks. Number two, what if I haven't filed my tax return for 2018 or 2019? Usually, the federal income tax filing due date is on April 15th. Because of the coronavirus pandemic, the IRS has extended the deadline to July 15th. If you haven't filed your 2019 tax return, the IRS will just use your 2018 tax return to determine the check amount. But if you haven't even filed your 2018 tax return yet, it's probably a good idea to file that now. You can file your taxes for free on the IRS website, and we will provide a link in the description. If you don't usually file your tax return because you don't meet the minimum income to file your taxes, you are still eligible for a check. The IRS is saying a simple tax return will be required. I believe we are. I believe you believe me. He got it straight for me, and I am telling the truth right now. I trust you. I believe you believe me. I believe you. I know your pain, I am asking you to follow through, believe me and I love you forever. I know your soul. I believe you believe me. I believe you. I believe you. I do believe you. I believe me. I believe you. I love you. A few things you need to know before we get into the details of how much you get. First, the check amount is based on your adjusted gross income, not your gross income. Adjusted gross income is your gross income minus all of the deductions you can get on your tax return. The IRS will either use your 2018 return or your 2019 return, which are the filings due in the current tax season, to determine the amount of your stimulus check You can find out your adjusted gross income In Box 7 of your 2018 1040 federal tax return And in box 8b on your 2019 1040 federal tax return Second the payment will be made based on your income level in 2018 or in 2019 as an estimate. The actual payment will be based on your 2020 tax return. So next year, if you file your 2020 tax return and find out your adjusted gross income is above the earning threshold for the stimulus check. You may have to pay back some or all of the funds. On the contrary, if your adjusted gross income in 2018 or 2019 disqualified you to get the check, but you lost your job in 2020. You won't get the check this year. However, you will get the rebate when you file your 2020 tax return. Now let's go over how much you might get. All single taxpayers earning up to $75,000 will receive $1,200.00. For each qualifying child under 17, you will receive $500.00. Head of household is usually a single parent, and earning up to $112,500 will receive $1,200.00 and $500.00 for each qualifying child under 17. Married taxpayers filing jointly and earning up to $150,000 will receive $2,400. For each qualifying child under 17, the couple will receive $500. Again, the earning is your adjusted gross income in 2018 or 2019. However, the check amount will decrease if you make more than the threshold. The checks decrease incrementally at 5%, or $5 for every additional $100 in income above the thresholds. The thresholds are $75,000 for single filers, $112,500 for head of household, and $150,000 for married couples filing jointly. So, for example, if you're a single filer and have an adjusted gross income of $75,100, instead of getting $1200 you will get $1,195. And you won't get any money or a check if your adjusted gross income is above the caps, which are $99,000 for single filers, $136,500 for head-of-household filers, and $198,000 for married couples filing jointly a few more things to note for 17 year olds and older adults who are claimed by their parents as a dependent on their tax return they are not eligible to receive the stimulus check and the parents will not get the $500 Child Credit either. For parents who have a newborn in 2020, you also won't get the $500 Child Credit this year but you will get the rebate when you filed your 2020 tax return next year. And if you want to find out exactly how much you will get without doing any calculation yourself, the Washington Post created a calculator on their website that you can use. We will include the link in our description. Number four, how do I apply for the stimulus check? If you qualify for the check, there's nothing you need to do or apply. The IRS will automatically send you the check based on the information on your tax return. There's no need for you to call the IRS and the IRS will not call you to ask for personal information. 5. Where are the check sent? If you have direct deposit information on your tax return, the IRS will send the check to the bank account number you provided. Or if you didn't have direct deposit information on your tax return, the IRS will email the check to the address you included on your tax return. So, if you moved after you filed your tax return and didn't have direct deposit information on your tax return, you should file form 882 with the IRS and a change of address notice with the US Postal Service as soon as possible. In addition for all Legal Permanent Residents, you also have to fill out the AR-11 form whenever you move. We will include all the links in the description. Number 6- When will I get my check? If you have Direct Deposit you will probably get the check within the next week or two. So keep an eye out and check your bank accounts. And if you've received your check, please leave us a comment. For people who don't have direct deposit, starting April 24th through September, the IRS will begin sending paper stimulus checks to the address on your tax return. The plan is to send paper stimulus checks to taxpayers with the lowest adjusted gross income. The IRS is also planning to create a new online portal that will enable taxpayers to update their direct deposit information and check the status of their stimulus check. As of right now, the new portal is not up and running yet. We will update you once we have more information, so make sure to check back. Number seven, do I need to pay tax for the amount I receive? No, the checks will not be taxed. Whatever amount you qualify for, you will receive that full amount. Number eight, If I owe past taxes, will my check be reduced? No. You will receive the full qualified amount. But remember, it's a good idea to pay off any overdue taxes before applying for citizenship. Because that's one of the indicators of good moral character. Number nine, if I receive the stimulus check, is it considered a public charge? The stimulus check is not considered a public charge under the USCIS's new rules that rolled out in February this year. The check is a 2020 tax credit paid in advance and thus does not fall under any benefit category in the public charge rule. So, it should not affect your eligibility to apply for a green card or citizenship. Last but not least, beware of scammers. You might receive an email asking you to click on a link to claim your stimulus check... Don't click it. Or you might get a phone call from the IRS asking you to verify your bank account and social security number. Hang up right away! The IRS will never send you an email to click on a link, or call you to verify your personal information. credit account, debit account or PayPal account information to anyone via phone, text, social media, email, or in person. And don't go to any website and enter your personal information because it promises to get your checks faster! The official government website always ends with .gov. Criminals will take every opportunity to perpetrate a fraud on unsuspecting victims. Therefore, it is important for you to remain vigilant. All right, that's it for today. Do you have any more questions? Leave us a comment. I'll see you next time. Bye!
